newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW-Sri Lanka paints rosy economic picture.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Sri Lanka paints rosy economic picture.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Central Bank painted a rosy picture of the economy in 1997 on Friday, saying it was possible to achieve robust six percent growth despite a dismal previous year.

Central Bank governor Amarananda Jayawardena told Reuters in an interview the growth pickup seen in the first half of 1997 would continue as the effect of lower lending rates spurred corporate investment.
"We are reasonably optimistic of achieving an overall growth rate of six percent this year," Jayawardena said.
High interest rates and a crippling drought allowed the country's economy to grow by only 3.8 percent in 1996, with both industrial and agricultural production hit badly.
Jayawardena said the situation had improved markedly this year, mainly because of easier monetary policy.
The Central Bank has reduced reserve ratios for banks twice since January, which has in turn brought prime lending rates down sharply.
They fell to an average 14.7 percent in the week to June 19 from 17.2 percent in the same period last year.
Jayawardena also said he expected average annual inflation to fall to between eight and nine percent this year against a peak of 15.9 last year as price pressures eased.
Inflation rose sharply last year after the government reduced administered prices, mainly the subsidy on wheat flour.
"Our concern now is whether the increase in credit and large capital inflows will tend to reignite inflationary pressures," he said.
Jayawardena added that the Central Bank was keeping a close watch on the situation and current credit expansion did not show an explosion in growth.

He said privatisation proceeds and capital inflow would help improve the government's financial position in 1997, and he expected an overall balance of payments (BoP) surplus after two years of deficit.
"The surplus should be around 180 million SDRs this year," he said. The BoP deficit was 62 million SDRs in 1996.
Overall, the government has said it aims to raise some five billion rupees ($85.6 million) by privatising state-run companies this year.

Sri Lanka has privatised several plantation companies this year and plans to bring strategic private investors into state-owned Sri Lanka Telecom by selling partial equity. "Proceeds from privatisation will help reduce government debt," Jayawardena said. But he said Sri Lanka was discussing with the International Monetary Fund the possibility of a $350 million loan under its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF).
"The ESAF is important to us because some of our economic problems cannot be changed overnight, they are long-term structural adjustments," the Central Bank governor said.

"We are moving towards low taxes, low tariffs, (and) growth and liberalisation of the market and containing military and other expenditure. I think we have the basic ingredients for a good ESAF programme," Jayawardena said.
He said if there was a settlement of Sri Lanka's ethnic conflicts, the economy should be able to achieve eight to 10 percent growth without overheating.
It should also be possible to lower the budget deficit to between four and five percent of gross domestic product, he said. The ratio stood at around 8.9 percent in 1996.
Sri Lankan troops are fighting a 13-year-old war with Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, who are demanding a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east.
But Jayawardena said if the war continued, the country faced higher inflation and the economy would only be able to grow at around six percent at most.
